# Smart Grid
The smart grid protects important station systems when power is scarce. It monitors each power network and deliberately turns off lower-priority devices before a shortage becomes a station-wide brownout.
Smart-grid shedding does not create power. A network can still brown out if it cannot physically supply the loads that remain enabled, either due to being considered essential or due to manual overrides.
## Availability levels
Every eligible powered device belongs to one of five availability levels. The grid supplies every level at or below its current availability ceiling. [color=green]General[/color] is the normal, fully available state. As the ceiling falls, higher-numbered levels are shed first.

This order means a shortage normally removes general machinery first, followed by lights, shuttle systems, and Life Support. Essential Systems are kept online as long as the physical power network can support them.
A wire network's effective availability is limited by its own local ceiling and the applicable signals feeding it. Batteries and generators on the same network can support one another, while a more restrictive relay or manual output can still lower the network's availability.
## Automatic shedding
The smart grid watches generation, battery reserves, and output limits on each network. A shortage must persist briefly before a level is shed, which prevents momentary generator ramping or a transient load spike from cycling equipment off and on.
Recovery is deliberately slower. After a network remains free of shortages for a sustained period, it restores one level at a time. If the shortage continues, the grid instead sheds another level. Fix the underlying deficit by bringing generation online, reducing demand, restoring damaged cables, or charging depleted storage.
### Generators
An enabled generator sends General availability while it is ramping up, then asks the grid to reduce demand only after it has remained at its own output limit. This ensures that it gets sufficient demand to continue ramping rather than settling below the output it could otherwise support. Disabled generators and generators producing no power send no availability signal.
### Power Network Batteries
SMESes, substations, and APCs are power network batteries. Their behavior is split based on whether they're in [bold]Primary Mode[/bold] or [bold]Reserve Mode[/bold]. A device is in [bold]Reserve Mode[/bold] when its input is supplied through an upstream power-network battery with its output breaker enabled. Otherwise, it is in [bold]Primary Mode[/bold].
In [bold]Reserve Mode[/bold], a battery will generally forward the availability signal it receives from its input network. This means that its battery storage is generally not touched unless the upstream batteries are fully drained (at which point it will expend its charge to power whatever demands are still online downstream).
In [bold]Primary Mode[/bold], a battery will proactively attempt to increase the availability level of its downstream network by using its stored energy. Each availability level has a cutoff threshold. Below that threshold, a discharging [bold]Primary Mode[/bold] battery trips a reserve breaker and sheds that level. Until it sheds a level, a [bold]Primary Mode[/bold] battery continues to provide the highest availability level it has not shed. Once a level is shed, the battery will not restore that level until it has recharged to the higher recovery threshold for that availability level. This hysteresis reduces rapid cycling of availability levels.
### Power Consumers
Power consumers are each assigned an availability level, and will stop consuming network power if the availability level of their input network is below their assigned level. They may continue to consume power if they have an internal battery of their own.
## Manual controls
### Reserve breakers
For batteries in [bold]Primary Mode[/bold], there are dashed outlines on the charge meter that indicate the thresholds for shedding and recovering. Clicking an active region trips that breaker and every higher availability level. Clicking a tripped region instead recovers that breaker and every lower level.
This is separate from an output availability override and is not persistent: automatic reserve logic can trip the breaker again almost immediately. It is most useful when the charge level is within the trip region, or when sufficient upstream generation is actively charging the battery.
### Output availability overrides
Portable generators, SMESes, substations, and APCs have a Smart Grid Availability control in their interface. It lists the availability levels from General at the top to Essential Systems at the bottom.
- The left [color=cyan]->[/color] marks availability received from the input network. - The right [color=cyan]->[/color] marks availability sent to the output network. - A solid outline marks a manual selection.
Select a level to override automatic availability for that device's output network. This is useful for retaining service to a critical room during an emergency, or for deliberately shedding a downstream area. Selecting the same level again returns the device to automatic operation.
When the device returns to automatic load shedding from a manual override, it does so at the level that was selected when the override was cleared. This allows for setting a temporary override and then unsetting it after power is restored to recover a network more quickly than it would naturally scale back up.
## Inspecting the grid
Use a multitool on an anchored power cable to inspect that cable's network. In addition to normal power statistics, the report shows:
- Current availability and local availability. - Whether the grid is stable, preparing to shed, or preparing to recover. - The immediate sources supplying that network and whether they are healthy, output-capped, low on reserve, or disabled.
The Power Monitoring Computer also shows smart-grid status for its focused power devices. Inspect the HV network for station-wide causes, then follow through SMES, substation, and APC boundaries to isolate the affected area.
## Responding to a power emergency
- Communicate! Although telecommunications equipment is load-shed early, handheld radios will continue to work. - Inspect the affected network with a multitool or the Power Monitoring Computer. - Determine whether the problem is insufficient generation, a drained or capped battery, or a broken/disconnected supply path. - Restore generation or storage capacity before relying on manual overrides. - If needed, use a nearby APC, substation, SMES, or portable generator to choose a temporary availability level for the affected output network. - Return the control to automatic operation once the underlying fault is resolved.
